intent: I'm hiking a high mountain route in January and I refuse to come back with only phone pictures again. My pack budget gives me maybe a kilo for camera gear including spares. Here's what confuses me: everyone says bigger sensors handle dim alpine dawns better, but bigger sensors seem to mean heavier lenses, and I don't understand why the two are physically linked or how much sensor I can carry within my weight limit. Winter shooters must have hard-won opinions on what actually survives freezing ridges and gloved hands. I want something light and cold-tolerant that still catches low sun, and I'd love your single concrete pick with whatever keeps it alive up there.
author_notes: Deep-tier task generated by gen_task_spec.py from configs/deep_topics/coral_bleaching_causal.yaml. Golden: must=135, pool=689.
intent_v1_legacy: I went snorkeling somewhere I'd visited years ago and the reef looked ghostly white and half dead, and it genuinely shook me. I want to actually understand why coral bleaching is speeding up, not just 'climate change' as a slogan but the real chain of it, from what's happening in the water's temperature and chemistry all the way down to the coral itself dying off. And are some coral species holding up better than others? Walk me through how it all connects, and whether anything people are doing actually helps.

tri_source.angle: Camera for a cold, weight-limited mountain trek: freezing batteries, gloved hands, and pack weight change the answer
